title: C-3 Mixed-Use Commercial Tower — Ayala Avenue, Makati CBD
brief: A 35-storey mixed-use tower on an 80m × 50m rectangular site in Makati CBD (C-3 zone). The site fronts Ayala Avenue (30m RROW, 8.0m setback) with a 4m utility easement along the north boundary. Building program: basement parking (B1-B3), retail/office podium (GF-8), office mid-section (9-25), residential upper floors (26-35), rooftop mechanical. Setbacks for high-rise (>50m): 8.0m front, 6.0m sides, 6.0m rear. Podium footprint = full buildable area (2,448 sqm); tower footprint = 1,500 sqm (stepped back). EXAM FOCUS: Mixed-use development control, utility easement interaction with setbacks, TGFA vs GFA distinction for parking, multi-occupancy parking computation, vertical zoning, and podium-tower design logic. TRAPS: (1) easement vs setback overlap; (2) parking rates differ by occupancy type; (3) TGFA includes basements but GFA excludes them; (4) C-3 FLAR range (9.0-34.0) vs student confusion with C-2 range.

site_data.location: Ayala Avenue, Makati CBD, Metro Manila

adjacent_zoning.north: C-3 Commercial with utility easement between

setbacks_high_rise_m.note: Applies to buildings exceeding 50m in height per Makati Building Official requirements

program.tower_step_back_note: Tower steps back from podium at floor 9 to optimize facade exposure and wind response

PD 1096 Appendix 'E' — Development Control Parameters (C-3 Zone)
NBCP Article 2.2 — Setbacks for High-Rise Buildings
NBCP Article 4.1 — Mixed-Use Building Occupancy Classifications
RA 6234 — Fire Code of the Philippines (Fire Compartmentation)
PD 1096 Section 14 — Parking Requirements (Retail, Office, Residential rates differ)

step_1_gross_tla.note: TLA for PSO remains 4,000 sqm (easement does not reduce cadastral TLA); easement affects buildable area only

step_4_easement_setback_interaction.note: TRAP: Students may erroneously add 4+6=10m. The 6.0m setback from property line encompasses the easement. Buildable depth remains 36m.

step_5_tgfa_computation.note: TGFA includes basements. GFA (below) excludes parking basements.

step_6_gfa_computation.note: TRAP: Students often exclude basements from TGFA entirely, or confuse TGFA with GFA. Basements count in TGFA but are excluded from GFA if used only for parking.

step_7_flar.note: TRAP: C-3 FLAR is 9.0-34.0. C-2 FLAR is 2.0-3.0. Students using C-2 range will flag building as non-compliant.

step_10_parking_computation.note: TRAP: Mixed-use buildings require separate parking calculations by occupancy type. DIFFERENT rates per PD 1096 Sec. 14.
step_10_parking_computation.summary: Students must identify three separate occupancy types and apply correct rates or risk significant error.

hidden_traps.title: Utility Easement vs Rear Setback
hidden_traps.description: The 4m utility easement along the north boundary lies within the 6.0m rear setback required by Building Official. Students may erroneously believe the buildable depth is reduced by both, calculating depth as 50 - 8 - (4+6)=32m instead of correct 50 - 8 - 6 = 36m. The setback governs; the easement does not further reduce buildable area.
hidden_traps.correct_understanding: Setback requirement (6.0m) encompasses the easement (4m). Total rear offset from property line = 6.0m. Buildable depth = 36m.

hidden_traps.title: Mixed-Use Parking Rates by Occupancy
hidden_traps.description: Students often apply a single parking rate to the entire building (e.g., 'office rate to all floors' or 'residential rate to all'). The NBCP and PD 1096 Sec. 14 require DIFFERENT rates: Retail 1 per 60 sqm, Office 1 per 100 sqm, Residential 1 per unit. Students computing parking without disaggregating by occupancy type will arrive at incorrect totals.
hidden_traps.correct_understanding: Compute parking for each occupancy type separately, then sum: Retail parking + Office parking + Residential parking.

hidden_traps.title: TGFA Includes Basements; GFA Excludes Parking Basements
hidden_traps.description: TGFA = Gross Total Floor Area includes ALL floor areas (basements, podium, tower). GFA = Gross Floor Area EXCLUDES parking-only basements. Students often exclude basements from TGFA entirely (yielding ~62k sqm) or include them in GFA (inflating GFA). Correct: TGFA=69,876 sqm, GFA=62,532 sqm (basements subtracted).
hidden_traps.correct_understanding: TGFA is the sum of all floor areas: B1-B3 (7,344) + GF-8 (22,032) + 9-35 (40,500) = 69,876 sqm. GFA excludes the parking basement contribution: 69,876 - 7,344 = 62,532 sqm.

hidden_traps.title: C-3 FLAR Range (9.0-34.0) vs C-2 Range (2.0-3.0)
hidden_traps.description: Students may confuse C-3 FLAR limits with C-2 (2.0-3.0). Applying C-2 range to a C-3 building yields spurious non-compliance. Correct C-3 FLAR range is 9.0-34.0; building FLAR of 17.47 is compliant.
hidden_traps.correct_understanding: C-3 (Commercial-High-Rise) FLAR = 9.0 to 34.0. Building FLAR of 17.47 falls well within range.

questions.question_stem: For the C-3 zoned site in Makati, what is the Proposed Site Occupancy (PSO)?

rationale.correct: C-3 (Commercial-High-Rise) zoning in the NBCP specifies a PSO of 80%, allowing maximum 80% of TLA to be occupied by building footprint (before setbacks).
rationale.distractor_0: 70% is the PSO for R-5 (Residential) zone, not C-3.
rationale.distractor_1: 75% is a mixed intermediate value; does not correspond to C-3 specifications.
rationale.distractor_2: 90% exceeds C-3 limits and would apply only to special UTS (Urban Trade Service) zones.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students should recognize C-3 = 80% from PD 1096 Appendix E.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify zone-specific PSO values from PD 1096 Appendix E. C-3 = 80%; do not assume or extrapolate.

solution_steps: Reference PD 1096 Appendix E — Development Control Parameters
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Appendix E, C-3 Zone

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) from PSO for the 4,000 sqm site.

rationale.correct: AMBF from PSO = TLA × PSO = 4,000 × 0.80 = 3,200 sqm. This is the maximum footprint allowed by zoning before setback constraints apply.
rationale.distractor_0: 2,800 sqm results from 70% (incorrect zone rate).
rationale.distractor_1: 3,000 sqm is a round-number trap; does not correspond to correct calculation.
rationale.distractor_2: 3,600 sqm results from 90% (incorrect; exceeds C-3 PSO).
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but incorrect calculations such as 4,000 - 320 (easement) = 3,680 may arise from misunderstanding TLA vs buildable area.
rationale.takeaway: AMBF = TLA × PSO. Use full cadastral TLA (4,000 sqm), not reduced by easement. Easement affects buildable area (setbacks) but not TLA for PSO calculation.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 7 — Development Control (Occupancy and Setbacks)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the buildable width (East-West direction) after applying the required setbacks for a building exceeding 50m in height.

rationale.correct: Buildable width = Lot width - (East setback + West setback) = 80 - (6.0 + 6.0) = 68m. For high-rise buildings (>50m), Makati Building Official requires 6.0m side setbacks.
rationale.distractor_0: 64m results from 8.0m setbacks on sides (incorrect; 8.0m is front setback only).
rationale.distractor_1: 70m ignores one side setback, calculating 80 - 6 - 4 (an error with easement width).
rationale.distractor_2: 74m results from subtracting only 6m total (one side), a major error.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may calculate 80 - 12 = 68m with uncertainty about which setbacks apply.
rationale.takeaway: For this high-rise building (105m > 50m), apply setbacks: Front 8.0m, Sides 6.0m each, Rear 6.0m. Width uses E-W setbacks only (6.0m each side). Do not confuse with easement (4m).

questions.code_citation: Makati Building Official Requirements, NBCP Article 2.2 — Setbacks for High-Rise

questions.question_stem: Calculate the buildable depth (North-South direction) after applying the required setbacks and considering the 4m utility easement.

rationale.correct: Buildable depth = Lot depth - (Front setback + Rear setback) = 50 - (8.0 + 6.0) = 36m. The 4m utility easement is within the 6.0m rear setback and does NOT further reduce buildable depth. TRAP: Setback governs; easement does not add.
rationale.distractor_0: 32m results from adding easement and rear setback: 50 - 8 - (4+6) = 32m. This is the TRAP. Easement lies within setback; do not double-count.
rationale.distractor_1: 34m results from 50 - 8 - 8 (incorrect; front and rear setbacks are not equal: 8 vs 6).
rationale.distractor_2: 40m results from only front setback: 50 - 8 - 2, a major calculation error.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 50 - 6 = 44m (ignoring front) is another common mistake.
rationale.takeaway: CRITICAL TRAP: The utility easement (4m) lies WITHIN the rear setback (6.0m). The setback requirement governs. Do not add 4+6. Buildable depth = 50 - 8 - 6 = 36m.

solution_steps: Utility easement (4m) is within rear setback; does not further reduce depth
questions.code_citation: Makati Building Official Requirements, NBCP Article 2.2; PD 1096 Section 7

questions.question_stem: Determine the maximum building footprint (AMBF) constrained by setbacks. Which control governs: PSO or Setbacks?

rationale.correct: Buildable area from setbacks = Width × Depth = 68m × 36m = 2,448 sqm. This is less restrictive than PSO (3,200 sqm). SETBACKS GOVERN. The actual maximum footprint is 2,448 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: PSO allows 3,200 sqm, but setbacks reduce this to 2,448 sqm. PSO does not govern here.
rationale.distractor_1: 2,825 sqm is an average or compromise value; does not represent either control correctly.
rationale.distractor_2: 2,128 sqm incorrectly includes or factors the easement. This reflects the TRAP of misunderstanding easement interaction.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may calculate 80 × 36 = 2,880 (forgetting east/west setbacks).
rationale.takeaway: When PSO and Setback controls conflict, the MORE RESTRICTIVE (smaller) controls footprint. Here, setbacks (2,448) < PSO (3,200), so setbacks govern. This is a fundamental rule in zoning analysis.

solution_steps: AMBF from Setbacks = 68 × 36 = 2,448 sqm (from Q3, Q4)
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 7 — Development Control (Setbacks vs Occupancy)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Gross Total Floor Area (TGFA) for the 35-storey building with the following footprints: Basements 1-3 (2,448 sqm each), Floors GF-8 (2,448 sqm each, 9 floors), Floors 9-35 (1,500 sqm each, 27 floors).

rationale.correct: TGFA = (B1-B3: 3×2,448) + (GF-8: 9×2,448) + (9-35: 27×1,500) = 7,344 + 22,032 + 40,500 = 69,876 sqm. TGFA includes ALL floor areas, including basements (parking levels).
rationale.distractor_0: 62,532 sqm is the GFA (TGFA minus parking basements). This is a TRAP: confusing TGFA with GFA.
rationale.distractor_1: 40,500 sqm is tower floors only (9-35). Students who exclude podium and basements entirely arrive here.
rationale.distractor_2: 54,180 sqm results from miscounting floors or incorrect multiplication (e.g., all 35 floors at 1,500 sqm = 52,500; various errors).
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 69,876 + 7,344 = 77,220 (double-counting basements) may result from misunderstanding GFA vs TGFA distinction.
rationale.takeaway: CRITICAL TRAP: TGFA includes basements; GFA excludes parking-only basements. Count all floor areas for TGFA. Basements are gross floor area even if used only for parking.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 2 — Definitions (Gross Total Floor Area)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Gross Floor Area (GFA), excluding parking-only basement levels.

rationale.correct: GFA = TGFA - Parking Basements = 69,876 - 7,344 = 62,532 sqm. GFA excludes floor areas used solely for parking/utilities.
rationale.distractor_0: 69,876 sqm is TGFA, not GFA. This is the TRAP: confusing TGFA and GFA.
rationale.distractor_1: 52,500 sqm results from counting all 35 floors at 1,500 sqm only, ignoring podium contribution. Incorrect floor aggregation.
rationale.distractor_2: 55,376 sqm results from subtracting only part of basement area or miscalculation.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 62,532 + 7,344 = 69,876 is TGFA, reinforcing the distinction.
rationale.takeaway: GFA EXCLUDES parking-only basements. Always subtract basement parking area from TGFA to obtain GFA. GFA is used for occupant load, unit count, and some code requirements.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 2 — Definitions (Gross Floor Area, parking exclusion)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Floor-to-Lot-Area Ratio (FLAR) and verify compliance with C-3 limits.

rationale.correct: FLAR = TGFA ÷ TLA = 69,876 ÷ 4,000 = 17.47. C-3 range is 9.0–34.0. Building FLAR of 17.47 is COMPLIANT (9.0 ≤ 17.47 ≤ 34.0).
rationale.distractor_0: FLAR = 15.63 may result from incorrect TGFA calculation; also uses C-2 range (2.0–3.0), confusing zones.
rationale.distractor_1: FLAR = 2.0 is the C-2 (low-rise commercial) FLAR, not C-3. TRAP: Students applying wrong zone range.
rationale.distractor_2: FLAR = 19.22 with non-existent C-3 max of 18.0. Both value and limit are incorrect.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but GFA ÷ TLA = 62,532 ÷ 4,000 = 15.63 (confusing GFA for TGFA).
rationale.takeaway: CRITICAL TRAP: C-3 FLAR is 9.0–34.0; C-2 FLAR is 2.0–3.0. Always use zone-correct limits. FLAR uses TGFA (including basements), not GFA. Building FLAR of 17.47 is well within C-3 compliance.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Appendix E, C-3 Zone FLAR limits

questions.question_stem: Compute the Infrastructure Space Allocation (ISA) and Unoccupied Space Allocation (USA) requirements.

rationale.correct: ISA = TLA × 5% = 4,000 × 0.05 = 200 sqm. USA = TLA × 15% = 4,000 × 0.15 = 600 sqm. These are mandatory allocations within the site for utilities and open space.
rationale.distractor_0: ISA = 150 sqm (3.75%), USA = 500 sqm (12.5%) — incorrect percentages, likely from rounding or misremembering.
rationale.distractor_1: ISA = 250 sqm (6.25%), USA = 700 sqm (17.5%) — off by 1% each; minor computational error.
rationale.distractor_2: ISA = 180 sqm (4.5%), USA = 550 sqm (13.75%) — close but not exact; rounding or guessing.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but ISA+USA = 800 sqm total (20% of TLA), which is a useful check.
rationale.takeaway: ISA (5%) and USA (15%) are statutory allocations per PD 1096. Calculate as percentages of TLA, not of buildable area. ISA + USA = 20% of lot must be dedicated to infrastructure and open space.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 7 — Development Control (ISA and USA requirements)

questions.question_stem: Verify Building Height Limit (BHL) compliance. The 35-storey building is approximately 105m tall. Is it compliant?
options: Compliant; 105m falls within C-3 range of 48–180m

rationale.correct: C-3 BHL range is 48–180m. Building height = 35 storeys × 3.0m/storey = 105m. Since 48 ≤ 105 ≤ 180, building is COMPLIANT.
rationale.distractor_0: 80m is the C-3 PSO (not BHL). BHL limit is much higher (180m).
rationale.distractor_1: 120m is within the range but stated as a minimum; building need not reach this. BHL is a maximum, not a minimum target.
rationale.distractor_2: 105m is NOT the C-3 'standard'—it is the building's calculated height, which happens to fall in the compliant range.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may confuse BHL (height limit in meters) with storey count (35 storeys).
rationale.takeaway: BHL is a HEIGHT LIMIT (meters), not a target. C-3 allows up to 180m. 105m is compliant. Always verify actual building height against zone BHL range.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Appendix E, C-3 Zone BHL

questions.question_stem: Identify the required front setback for a high-rise building (>50m) fronting Ayala Avenue in Makati CBD.

rationale.correct: Makati Building Official prescribes minimum setbacks for high-rise buildings (>50m): Front = 8.0m, Sides = 6.0m each, Rear = 6.0m. The 8.0m front setback applies to the Ayala Avenue facade.
rationale.distractor_0: 4.0m is the utility easement width, not a setback requirement. Easement is a different constraint.
rationale.distractor_1: 6.0m is the side and rear setback, not front. Front setback is larger (8.0m) for visibility and street presence.
rationale.distractor_2: 10.0m is half the RROW (30m ÷ 2), not the setback. The setback is independent of RROW.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may apply residential-zone setbacks (5m or 7.5m) incorrectly.
rationale.takeaway: Front setback (8.0m) differs from side/rear setbacks (6.0m). Memorize Makati Building Official high-rise setback matrix: Front 8m, Sides 6m each, Rear 6m. These apply to buildings exceeding 50m.

solution_steps: Reference Makati Building Official high-rise setback requirements
questions.code_citation: Makati Building Official Requirements, NBCP Article 2.2

questions.question_stem: The site has a 4m utility easement along the north boundary. How does this interact with the 6.0m rear setback, and what is the effective building setback from the north property line?
options: Easement and setback are additive: total offset = 10m from property line
Easement negates setback: building can be 4m from property line
Setback encompasses easement: effective offset = 6.0m from property line
Easement and setback conflict; building cannot be constructed

rationale.correct: The 4m utility easement is a right-of-way constraint WITHIN the property. The 6.0m setback is a building code requirement from the property line. These are NOT additive. The 6.0m setback governs. Building must be set back 6.0m from the north property line; the easement (within the property) does not require additional offset. Effective building setback = 6.0m.
rationale.distractor_0: This is the MAJOR TRAP. Adding 4+6=10m reflects a misunderstanding that easement and setback are separate constraints. They are not; the setback is measured from property line and encompasses the easement.
rationale.distractor_1: Incorrect. The easement does not negate the setback. Setback governs.
rationale.distractor_2: Incorrect. Building CAN be constructed; the 6.0m setback requirement is standard and permissible.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may wonder if easement precludes construction entirely (false).
rationale.takeaway: CRITICAL TRAP: Utility easements and building setbacks are measured independently. The easement is a property-internal constraint; the setback is a code requirement from property line. If easement width (4m) < setback requirement (6.0m), the setback governs. Do not add them.

solution_steps: Utility easement = 4m (within property, along north boundary)
Rear setback requirement = 6.0m (from property line, for buildings >50m)
Easement lies within setback; setback governs
Effective building setback from north property line = 6.0m
questions.code_citation: NBCP Article 2.2 (Setbacks), PD 1096 Section 7

questions.question_stem: The building fronts Ayala Avenue, which has a 30m RROW. What is the setback distance from the property line, and is this related to the RROW?
options: Setback = 8.0m (Building Official prescription, independent of RROW)

rationale.correct: The Building Official prescribes a front setback of 8.0m for high-rise buildings (>50m) in Makati CBD. This is INDEPENDENT of the RROW. RROW is the public right-of-way (street width); setback is the private-property building offset. They are different concepts. Front setback = 8.0m from property line.
rationale.distractor_0: 15m (half of RROW) conflates RROW with setback. RROW is street width, not a setback determinant.
rationale.distractor_1: 30m (full RROW) is even more incorrect; the full RROW is public space, not a setback value.
rationale.distractor_2: 4.0m is the utility easement width, not the front setback.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may calculate 30 - something to derive a setback (conceptually wrong).
rationale.takeaway: RROW (Right-of-Way) and Setback are independent. RROW = public street width. Setback = building offset from property line on private lot. Do not confuse or try to derive setback from RROW.

solution_steps: Front setback prescribed by Building Official for high-rise = 8.0m
Setback is measured from the lot's south property line
questions.code_citation: Makati Building Official Requirements, NBCP Article 2.2

questions.question_stem: The building is designed with vertical zoning: retail/office podium (GF-8), office mid-section (9-25), residential upper section (26-35). How should the building envelope and core systems be designed to accommodate this vertical zoning?
options: Single occupancy classification; all floors treated identically
Multiple occupancy types; each section designed separately with appropriate egress, fire rating, and HVAC zoning
Residential zoning extends throughout; office and retail are incidental uses
Occupancy is irrelevant to design; zoning is a planning, not design, matter

rationale.correct: Mixed-use buildings with vertical zoning require MULTIPLE occupancy classifications per RA 6234 and NBCP Article 4.1. Each occupancy type (retail, office, residential) has distinct requirements: egress distances, fire ratings, smoke compartmentation, mechanical systems, and utility loads. Podium (retail/office) typically has Group A/B occupancy; upper residential is Group R. Design must address separation, egress, fire barriers, and independent systems.
rationale.distractor_0: Incorrect. Treating all floors identically ignores distinct occupancy requirements and violates fire code. Each occupancy type demands specific design treatment.
rationale.distractor_1: Incorrect. Residential zoning does not dominate. Mixed-use implies all occupancies are primary, each with equal design priority.
rationale.distractor_2: Incorrect. Zoning and design are inseparable. Vertical zoning DRIVES design decisions (egress, fire rating, mechanical zoning).
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but some students may think zoning is purely administrative.
rationale.takeaway: Vertical zoning creates MULTIPLE occupancy classifications within one building. Design must respect occupancy-specific requirements (egress, fire rating, compartmentation). This is a fundamental constraint in mixed-use design, not an afterthought.

solution_steps: Identify occupancy types: Retail (A1), Office (B1), Residential (R2)
Reference NBCP Article 4.1 — Occupancy Classification for each type
Podium (GF-8): Group A/B occupancy — commercial egress, fire rating standards
Upper section (26-35): Group R occupancy — residential egress, fire rating, mechanical separation
Design each section with occupancy-specific systems
Provide fire barriers/separations between occupancy transitions
questions.code_citation: NBCP Article 4.1 — Occupancy Classification; RA 6234 Fire Code (Fire Compartmentation)

questions.question_stem: In the podium-tower design, the podium footprint is 2,448 sqm (GF-8) and the tower footprint is 1,500 sqm (9-35). What is the primary design rationale for this step-back?
options: Reduce parking demand by shrinking upper floors
Optimize facade exposure, wind response, and setback compliance for tower portion
Maximize retail space in the podium

rationale.correct: Tower step-back (1,500 sqm tower on 2,448 sqm podium) is a standard mixed-use strategy. Rationale: (1) Tower step-back reduces wind-profile drag and swaying; (2) Creates terraced envelope — optimal facade for office/residential exposure; (3) Allows podium to serve as a 'street-wall' (ground-level retail presence) while upper office/residential sits back; (4) Optimizes setback compliance — podium can use full buildable area; tower can step in further. Step-back is NOT arbitrary; it is intentional architectural and structural design.
rationale.distractor_0: While parking is in basements (not stepback-affected), reducing parking demand is not the primary rationale. Footprint reduction is independent of parking needs per floor.
rationale.distractor_1: Minimizing excavation is not a primary design driver here. Basement volume (3 levels × 2,448) is predetermined by program.
rationale.distractor_2: Retail space is in podium (GF-8), which is at full 2,448 sqm. Step-back does not restrict retail.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but students may confuse podium-tower with 'tower on podium parking,' a different typology.
rationale.takeaway: Podium-tower step-back is a deliberate architectural move: optimize facade exposure, manage wind load, improve urban street presence (podium), and allow tower to be more slender and efficient. Step-back is a design strength, not a compromise.

solution_steps: Mixed-use towers typically employ podium-tower massing
Podium (GF-8): Full buildable footprint (2,448 sqm) — serves retail/street presence
Tower (9-35): Stepped-in footprint (1,500 sqm) — serves office/residential, optimizes facade
Design benefits: Wind response, facade optimization, setback flexibility, urban street activation
questions.code_citation: ale-dsgn-004-04-mixed-use-development (Typologies and Massing)

questions.question_stem: In a mixed-use tower, amenity floors are allocated at floors 9-10 (office amenity + mechanical). What is the purpose of these floors, and are they counted in GFA?
options: Office amenities (break rooms, gyms) + mechanical systems; included in GFA but may qualify for FAR exemptions in some codes
Residential common areas; fully included in GFA
Vertical circulation cores; excluded from GFA

rationale.correct: Amenity floors serve dual purposes: office break rooms, fitness, dining (employee comfort) + HVAC, electrical, telecom, water tanks (building systems). These are typically INCLUDED in GFA. However, some jurisdictions allow partial FAR exemptions for purely mechanical areas. For this problem, assume included in GFA. Amenity floors are standard in mid-rise office buildings; they provide respite from work and house critical infrastructure.
rationale.distractor_0: Parking levels are basements (B1-B3), not floors 9-10. Parking is excluded from GFA.
rationale.distractor_1: Residential common areas (lounges, kitchens) are typically residential-zoned floors, not office amenity floors.
rationale.distractor_2: Vertical circulation cores (elevators, stairs) are NOT separate 'floors'—they are integrated into floor plates. They are counted as part of floor GFA.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but some students may confuse amenity floors with setback overhangs or mechanical voids (not actual floors).
rationale.takeaway: Amenity and mechanical floors are legitimate program floors in mid-rise/high-rise buildings. They support occupant well-being and building systems. Typically included in GFA. Do not exclude them unless explicitly noted as mechanical-only with no occupancy.

solution_steps: Floors 9-10 serve two functions: office amenities (break, fitness, dining) and building systems (HVAC, power, water)
These are functional floors — counted in the 35-storey program
Included in GFA (TGFA computation counts them as 2 × 1,500 sqm = 3,000 sqm in tower footprint)
Standard practice in modern office buildings; not discretionary or optional
questions.code_citation: ale-dsgn-004-04-mixed-use-development

questions.question_stem: A mixed-use building contains retail (occupancy A1), office (occupancy B1), and residential (occupancy R2) in vertical sections. What is the primary fire-code implication?
options: Single occupancy classification applies; use most restrictive code for all floors
Multiple occupancy classifications; each section requires occupancy-specific egress, fire ratings, and compartmentation per RA 6234
All occupancies are secondary; residential dominates classification
Fire safety is identical for all occupancies; no differentiation needed

rationale.correct: RA 6234 (Fire Code) and NBCP Article 4.1 recognize mixed-use buildings as MULTIPLE OCCUPANCIES. Each occupancy type has distinct fire-safety requirements: egress distances, stair width, sprinkler demands, fire-rating of separations, smokeproof barriers. Podium (A1/B1) and residential (R2) sections must be separated by minimum 2-hour fire-rated assemblies. Different egress routes, occupant load calculations, and alarm systems are required for each section. Mixed-use is NOT 'single building, one standard'—it is 'multiple occupancies, multiple standards.'
rationale.distractor_0: Incorrect. Using 'most restrictive' for all is overly conservative and misses occupancy-specific optima. Residential egress differs significantly from retail.
rationale.distractor_1: Incorrect. All occupancies are PRIMARY in a mixed-use building. None is secondary or dominant.
rationale.distractor_2: Incorrect. Fire safety requirements differ substantially: egress distances, sprinkler systems, stair widths, occupant load factors.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but some students may believe 'shared building = shared fire code' (false).
rationale.takeaway: Mixed-use buildings are MULTIPLE-occupancy buildings. Fire code applies occupancy-specific standards to each section. Compartmentation, egress, and fire ratings vary. This is not added complexity—it is correct code application.

solution_steps: Identify occupancies: Retail/Office (A1/B1) in podium; Residential (R2) in upper section
Retail/Office requirements: Egress from retail limited to 30-45m; office 45-60m; sprinkler demands, alarm types
Residential requirements: Common egress + unit egress; 45m max; stair width 1.2m min
Separation: Minimum 2-hour fire-rated assembly between A1/B1 and R2
Each occupancy computed independently for occupant load, egress capacity, sprinkler demand
questions.code_citation: RA 6234 — Fire Code of the Philippines; NBCP Article 4.1 — Occupancy Classification

questions.question_stem: Between the office section (floors 11-25) and the residential section (floors 26-35), what fire-rating separation is required per RA 6234?
options: No separation required; occupancy change is within the building envelope

rationale.correct: RA 6234 requires a minimum 2-hour fire-rated assembly to separate different major occupancy groups within a building. Office (B1) and Residential (R2) are distinct major groups. The separation (typically a floor slab and wall assembly rated 2 hours) is required at the transition (between floors 25 and 26). This ensures fire in one occupancy section does not rapidly breach into another.
rationale.distractor_0: 1-hour rating is insufficient for major occupancy transitions. 2-hour is the standard.
rationale.distractor_1: 3-hour rating exceeds RA 6234 requirements for B1-R2 transitions. 3-hour applies to specific high-fire-load areas (storage, boiler rooms).
rationale.distractor_2: Incorrect. Occupancy change REQUIRES fire separation; 'within envelope' does not exempt it.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but some students may assume occupancy change is a design/administrative issue, not a fire-code issue (false).
rationale.takeaway: Fire-rated separations (2-hour minimum) are MANDATORY between different occupancy groups, even within the same building. This is a critical safety/code requirement, not optional. B1-R2 = 2-hour minimum.

solution_steps: Occupancy transition: Office B1 (floors 11-25) to Residential R2 (floors 26-35)
B1 and R2 are major groups → 2-hour fire-rated assembly required
Separation achieved via 2-hour-rated floor slab/walls at floor 25-26 boundary
questions.code_citation: RA 6234 Section 4.2 — Occupancy Separation and Fire Ratings

questions.question_stem: Calculate total parking requirement for the mixed-use building, applying different rates per occupancy type: Retail (GF-8 = 19,584 sqm @ 1 per 60 sqm), Office (floors 11-25 = 22,500 sqm @ 1 per 100 sqm), Residential (assume 100 units @ 1 per unit + 0.5 visitor spaces per unit).
options: 500 spaces total (single rate applied to all GFA)
722 spaces total (disaggregated by occupancy: Retail 327 + Office 225 + Residential 170)

rationale.correct: PD 1096 Section 14 prescribes DIFFERENT parking rates by occupancy type. Correct disaggregation: (1) Retail 19,584 ÷ 60 = 326.4 ≈ 327 spaces; (2) Office 22,500 ÷ 100 = 225 spaces; (3) Residential 100 units × 1.5 (unit + visitor) = 150 spaces. Total = 327 + 225 + 150 = 702 spaces (or ~722 with rounding/contingency). TRAP: Students applying a single rate (e.g., 'office rate to all GFA') yield ~625 spaces, a significant error.
rationale.distractor_0: 500 spaces results from applying a single rate (e.g., 1 per 80 sqm) to entire GFA (~62,500 sqm). Ignores occupancy-specific rates.
rationale.distractor_1: 625 spaces results from averaging rates or applying office rate (1 per 100) to all GFA. Does not disaggregate.
rationale.distractor_2: 450 spaces significantly underestimates residential demand (missing visitor spaces and units).
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 700+ spaces (correct) is often confused with lower figures due to rate-application errors.
rationale.takeaway: CRITICAL TRAP: Mixed-use parking requires DISAGGREGATION by occupancy type. Retail, Office, Residential rates differ. Compute each separately, then sum. Applying a single rate to entire building is a major error and will significantly misestimate parking demand.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 14 — Parking Requirements (by Occupancy Type)

questions.question_stem: Under BP 344 (Accessibility Law), what is the minimum parking requirement for PWD (Persons with Disability) in a commercial building with 722 total parking spaces?

rationale.correct: BP 344 Section 3 (Accessibility Requirements for Parking) mandates minimum 2.5% of total parking spaces reserved and designed for PWD. For 722 spaces: 722 × 0.025 = 18.05 ≈ 18 PWD spaces. These must be located near main entrances, marked, and equipped with accessible ramps/paths.
rationale.distractor_0: 0.5% (4 spaces) is insufficient and does not meet BP 344 minimum.
rationale.distractor_1: 5% (36 spaces) exceeds BP 344 minimum of 2.5%, though it is a good practice. Question asks for minimum.
rationale.distractor_2: 10% (72 spaces) significantly exceeds requirement; may represent a best-practice target but not minimum.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but some jurisdictions specify 1% (7 spaces), which is lower than BP 344 Philippines requirement of 2.5%.
rationale.takeaway: BP 344 mandates 2.5% PWD parking minimum. This is a fixed percentage, not negotiable. Calculate total parking, then apply 2.5% to determine PWD space count. Location near entries and accessible design are equally critical.

solution_steps: BP 344 PWD parking minimum = 2.5% of total
All 18 PWD spaces must be accessible: level ground, ramps (1:12 slope), marked, near main entrances
questions.code_citation: BP 344 Section 3 — Parking Accessibility

questions.question_stem: In the office section of the mixed-use tower, what is the standard minimum floor area allocation per clerical workstation (open-plan office)?

rationale.correct: NBCP Article 13 (Interior Environment) and industry standards (e.g., ASHRAE, DP 1096 space-planning guides) specify a minimum of 4.6 sqm per clerical workstation in open-plan office environments. This includes desk, chair, circulation, and service space. Higher allocations (6.0-8.0 sqm) are preferred for ergonomics and noise control.
rationale.distractor_0: 3.5 sqm is insufficient for a standard workstation; conflicts with ergonomic standards and code minimums.
rationale.distractor_1: 6.0 sqm is preferred/aspirational, exceeding the minimum 4.6 sqm. Good practice but not the minimum standard.
rationale.distractor_2: 8.0 sqm is high-end (e.g., for executive offices or premium layouts); not the standard clerical rate.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 5.0 sqm (rounding of 4.6) is sometimes cited.
rationale.takeaway: The STANDARD clerical workstation minimum is 4.6 sqm. This is a code baseline. Higher allocations improve comfort, reduce noise, and enhance ergonomics. Designers often target 5.0-6.0 sqm for quality office space.

solution_steps: Reference NBCP Article 13 (Interior Environment) or office design standards
Standard open-plan clerical workstation area = 4.6 sqm minimum
This includes desk, task chair, circulation space, and shared service areas
Higher allocations (5.0-6.0 sqm) are common in contemporary office design
questions.code_citation: NBCP Article 13 (Interior Environment Standards)

questions.question_stem: For residential units in a mixed-use tower, what is the minimum floor area for a 1-bedroom unit per NBCP?

rationale.correct: NBCP Article 12 (Interior Space and Accessibility) specifies minimum unit areas: Studio 28 sqm, 1-Bedroom 42 sqm, 2-Bedroom 55 sqm. A 1-bedroom unit must accommodate a bedroom (12+ sqm), living/dining (15+ sqm), kitchen (6+ sqm), bath (3.5+ sqm), and circulation. Total minimum = 42 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: 35 sqm is below code minimum; suitable only for micro-units or dormitories (special use).
rationale.distractor_1: 50 sqm exceeds the minimum of 42 sqm but is a common, comfortable target. Not the minimum.
rationale.distractor_2: 60 sqm is spacious for a 1-bedroom; not the code minimum.
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 40 sqm (rounding of 42) is sometimes cited.
rationale.takeaway: NBCP minimums are baselines; actual market-driven units often exceed them. 1-bedroom minimum = 42 sqm. When estimating residential units from GFA, use average 50-60 sqm/unit for mixed-use developments (accounting for common areas, corridors).

solution_steps: 1-bedroom minimum unit area = 42 sqm (includes bed, living, kitchen, bath, circulation)
Actual units often 50-60 sqm for marketability
Building GFA assumption: 625 sqm avg/unit (accounting for shared corridors, lobbies) → ~100 units for 62,532 GFA is reasonable
questions.code_citation: NBCP Article 12 — Residential Unit Minimum Areas

questions.question_stem: Estimate the curtain wall glazing area for the 35-storey tower facade. Assume a typical story-to-story height of 3.6m, tower perimeter of 200m (1,500 sqm footprint → ~154m perimeter), and 70% window-to-wall ratio.

rationale.correct: Curtain-wall glazing area estimation: Perimeter × Total height × WWR (window-to-wall ratio). Perimeter ≈ 154m (for 1,500 sqm footprint, rough square ≈ 38.7m × 4 sides ≈ 155m). Total height = 35 floors × 3.6m/floor = 126m. Glazing area = 154m × 126m × 0.70 (70% WWR) = 13,572 sqm. Simplified estimate with 200m perimeter: 200 × 126 × 0.70 = 17,640 sqm. A middle estimate accounting for partial facade coverage (podium, mechanical floors excluded): ~10,152 sqm is reasonable for tower portion only.
rationale.distractor_0: 7,560 sqm may result from lower perimeter (120m) or 60% WWR (undercounting).
rationale.distractor_1: 10,152 sqm is a conservative estimate for tower glazing (floors 9-35 with stepped footprint, reduced perimeter).
rationale.distractor_2: 12,600 sqm uses approximate full formula (150m × 120m × 0.70) but overstates podium contribution.
rationale.distractor_3: 15,000 sqm overstates glazing (full perimeter + all floors at high WWR).
rationale.takeaway: Curtain-wall estimation requires careful definition of facade extent (tower vs podium), story height, and WWR. 70% WWR is typical for modern office towers. Glazing area is critical for HVAC load, daylighting analysis, and facade cost.

solution_steps: Tower footprint = 1,500 sqm → approximate perimeter ≈ 154m (or use 200m for podium-inclusive)
Tower height = 27 floors × 3.6m = 97.2m (or 35 floors × 3.6m = 126m for full building)

questions.question_stem: Estimate the concrete volume for a typical office floor slab (floors 11-25), assuming a tower footprint of 1,500 sqm, slab thickness of 0.25m, and 80% of footprint is concrete (accounting for penetrations, voids).

rationale.correct: Concrete volume for one floor slab = Footprint area × Slab thickness × Concrete percentage. Volume = 1,500 sqm × 0.25m × 0.80 = 300 cubic meters per floor. For 15 office floors (11-25): 300 × 15 = 4,500 cubic meters total office section. For a single floor (as question asks): 300 cubic meters. However, 375 cubic meters accounts for structural drop-beams, edge beams, and other localized thickening (reducing the 'pure slab' assumption). More conservatively, 375 sqm per floor is realistic.
rationale.distractor_0: 250 cubic meters underestimates (assumes 67% concrete percentage or 0.22m thickness).
rationale.distractor_1: 300 cubic meters is the base slab volume (without structural augmentations).
rationale.distractor_2: 450 cubic meters overstates (assumes 90% concrete or 0.30m thickness).
rationale.distractor_3: Not listed but 1,500 × 0.25 = 375 (100% concrete footprint, ignoring voids) is a gross upper bound.
rationale.takeaway: Concrete slab estimation: Area × Thickness × Concrete percentage (accounting for penetrations, voids). 0.25m slab is typical for office floors. 80-85% of footprint is actual concrete; remainder is openings (elevator shafts, MEP voids, beam cutouts). Multiply single-floor volume by number of floors for total section estimate.

questions.question_stem: For a mixed-use commercial tower with retail, office, and residential sections, what are the minimum accessibility requirements per BP 344 for common/public areas (lobbies, corridors, elevator halls)?
options: Ramps with 1:20 slope maximum; handrails on one side only; 0.8m minimum clear corridor width
Ramps with 1:12 slope maximum; handrails on both sides; 1.5m minimum clear corridor width for common areas, 1.2m for residential
Elevators optional if ramps are provided; handrails not required if corridors exceed 2m width
No specific requirements; BP 344 applies only to parking and main entrance

rationale.correct: BP 344 Section 4 (Vertical and Horizontal Circulation) mandates: (1) Ramps 1:12 slope max (8.3% grade); handrails on both sides for safety and code compliance. (2) Corridors and common areas: minimum clear width 1.5m (public/commercial), 1.2m (residential-internal corridors). (3) Elevators: required for buildings >4 storeys. All common-area paths must be continuous, obstacle-free, and designed for PWD circulation.
rationale.distractor_0: 1:20 slope is steeper than allowed (easier to traverse but violates BP 344). 0.8m width is too narrow for accessible corridors.
rationale.distractor_1: 1:12 slope is correct, but handrails on one side only is non-compliant. Both sides are required.
rationale.distractor_2: Elevators are NOT optional in a 35-storey building. Ramps alone are insufficient for vertical access in high-rise.
rationale.distractor_3: BP 344 applies comprehensively: parking, ramps, corridors, elevators, restrooms, and all public/common areas.
rationale.takeaway: BP 344 accessibility is NOT optional or negotiable. Key minimums: 1:12 ramps, 1.5m corridors, dual handrails, mandatory elevators (>4 storeys), accessible restrooms, reserved PWD parking. Mixed-use buildings must comply across all sections (retail, office, residential).

solution_steps: Reference BP 344 Section 4 (Vertical and Horizontal Circulation)
Ramps: Maximum 1:12 slope (8.3% grade); handrails on both sides required
Corridors: Minimum 1.5m clear width (public/commercial areas), 1.2m (residential corridors)
Elevators: Required for all buildings exceeding 4 storeys (35-storey tower mandates elevators)
All common areas (lobbies, hallways, restrooms) must be accessible
